📝 Chapter 20 — CNPA Practice Questions (Managed K8s)

Q1
Compare GKE, EKS, and AKS. What is each provider's key differentiator?
Show Answer
Answer

GKE: Pioneer (2015), Autopilot (serverless, pay-per-pod), free control plane, best GCP integration. EKS: AWS-native, Fargate for serverless pods, best IAM integration (IRSA), most market share. AKS: Azure-native, Automatic (managed nodes), best Azure AD integration, free control plane. Key: all three abstract control plane management — the cloud provider runs API server, etcd, scheduler. You manage worker nodes and workloads.

Explanation

CNPA Domain 4 tests managed K8s knowledge. Key differentiators: GKE Autopilot = serverless pods, EKS Fargate = serverless pods on AWS, AKS = best AD integration. "Which has free control plane?" → GKE + AKS. "Which has IRSA?" → EKS.

Q2
What is the shared responsibility model for managed K8s? What do YOU manage vs the cloud provider?
Show Answer
Answer

Cloud Provider: Control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager), etcd backups, control plane upgrades, control plane security patches. You: Worker nodes (unless serverless), pod networking (CNI), security policies (RBAC, NetworkPolicy, Kyverno), application deployments, data backups, monitoring, cost management. Shared: some providers offer managed node groups (EKS managed node groups, AKS node pools).

Explanation

CNPA exam: "Who manages etcd in EKS?" → AWS (it's part of control plane). "Who manages worker node security patches?" → YOU (unless using serverless/Fargate). The shared responsibility line moves with serverless — less for you to manage.

Q3
What is GKE Autopilot? How does it differ from Standard mode?
Show Answer
Answer

Autopilot is GKE's serverless mode: Google manages nodes (provisioning, scaling, patching). You deploy pods, Google handles everything else. Pay per pod (CPU/memory/storage), not per node. Differences from Standard: no node management (no node pools, no SSH), limited customization (no privileged pods, no hostNetwork), automatic upgrades, different pricing (per-pod vs per-node). Best for: teams wanting zero node operations, variable workloads, right-sized billing.

Explanation

CNPA exam: "Which GKE mode eliminates node management?" → Autopilot. "Pay per pod?" → Autopilot. Autopilot vs Standard is a key cost + operations trade-off. Autopilot = less control, less ops. Standard = more control, more ops.

Q4
What is IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) in EKS? Why is it better than static credentials?
Show Answer
Answer

IRSA maps K8s Service Accounts to AWS IAM roles via OIDC federation. Flow: Pod uses a labeled SA → EKS OIDC provider authenticates → AWS STS issues temporary credentials → Pod accesses AWS resources (S3, RDS, DynamoDB) with fine-grained permissions. No static AWS keys in K8s Secrets. Credentials auto-rotate. Each SA gets its own IAM role — least privilege at the pod level.

Explanation

CNPA exam: "How does EKS provide pod-level IAM?" → IRSA. This is the secure alternative to static IAM user keys. IRSA = OIDC + STS temporary credentials. Crossplane also uses IRSA for cloud provider authentication.

Q5
Compare EKS Fargate vs EKS Managed Node Groups. When choose each?
Show Answer
Answer

Fargate: Serverless — AWS runs a micro-VM per pod. No nodes visible. Pay per pod resources. Limited: no DaemonSets, no privileged pods, max 4 vCPU/30GB per pod. Best for: batch jobs, bursty workloads, simple stateless services. Managed Node Groups: AWS manages EC2 Auto Scaling groups. You see nodes (EC2 instances). Full K8s capabilities. Pay per EC2 instance. Best for: stateful workloads, DaemonSets (monitoring/logging agents), GPU workloads, maximum flexibility.

Explanation

CNPA exam: "Fargate vs Managed Node Groups?" → Fargate = serverless pods (no nodes), MNG = managed EC2 instances. Fargate is simpler but constrained. MNG is more flexible but requires node management awareness.

Q6
What is a multi-cloud platform strategy? How would anihpj run across EKS and GKE?
Show Answer
Answer

Multi-cloud = using multiple providers strategically, not running everything everywhere. anihpj strategy: Unified control plane: Backstage (portal) + ArgoCD (deploy to both) + Crossplane (provision infra on both) + Prometheus (federated metrics). Deployment: ArgoCD ApplicationSet deploys identical manifests to EKS (us-east-1) and GKE (us-central1). Routing: Route53 latency-based routing → nearest healthy cluster. Consistency: Same CI/CD, same observability, same security policies on both clouds.

Explanation

CNPA Domain 4: "What enables multi-cloud?" → Unified control plane (ArgoCD + Crossplane). Key: developers see ONE platform, not two clouds. The platform abstracts the cloud differences.

Q7
What is Cluster API (CAPI)? How does it enable declarative cluster management?
Show Answer
Answer

Cluster API is a CNCF project that manages K8s cluster lifecycle declaratively — using K8s CRDs to define clusters. Like K8s manages pods, CAPI manages clusters. You define a Cluster + MachineDeployment YAML, CAPI provisions VMs and bootstraps K8s. Supports: AWS, GCP, Azure, vSphere, bare metal. Enables: GitOps for clusters (ArgoCD manages Cluster API resources), self-service clusters (developer creates Cluster YAML → cluster provisioned).

Explanation

CNPA exam: "What manages K8s cluster lifecycle declaratively?" → Cluster API. CAPI brings the reconciliation loop to cluster management. Like Crossplane for cloud resources, CAPI for K8s clusters.

Q8
How do you upgrade a managed K8s cluster? Compare the process for GKE, EKS, AKS.
Show Answer
Answer

GKE: Automatic or manual upgrades. Select release channel (Rapid/Regular/Stable). Maintenance windows control timing. Node auto-upgrade (surge upgrade — creates new nodes, drains old). EKS: Manual control plane upgrade (AWS API/CLI). Node groups upgraded separately (launch template update + rolling replace). AKS: Automatic or manual. Planned maintenance windows. Node surge upgrade (similar to GKE). All: control plane upgraded first, then nodes. Always test in dev/staging before production.

Explanation

CNPA exam: "How are managed K8s clusters upgraded?" → Control plane first (provider handles), then worker nodes (you manage or auto-upgrade). GKE release channels + maintenance windows are key concepts. Always drain nodes before upgrade.

Q9
What are the cost implications of managed K8s? Compare GKE Autopilot vs EKS Standard costs for anihpj.
Show Answer
Answer

GKE Autopilot: Pay per pod (vCPU, memory, ephemeral storage). $0 management fee (free control plane). Example: 3 pods × 1 vCPU × 4GB = ~$75/month compute. EKS Standard: $0.10/hour control plane ($73/month) + EC2 instances. 3 × t3.large nodes = ~$120/month. Total: ~$193/month. Autopilot is cheaper for small workloads (pay only for pods). EKS is cheaper at scale (reserved instances, savings plans). Key: Autopilot = variable cost, EKS = fixed cost + variable cost.

Explanation

CNPA Domain 6 (cost). "Which is cheaper for small workloads?" → GKE Autopilot (no control plane fee, pay per pod). "Which for large, predictable workloads?" → EKS with reserved instances. Cloud cost is a platform engineering concern.

Q10
Design anihpj's multi-cloud architecture: EKS primary + GKE DR, with unified platform management.
Show Answer
Answer

Infrastructure: Terraform provisions EKS (us-east-1) + GKE (us-central1). Crossplane provisions RDS (AWS) + Cloud SQL (GCP). Deployment: ArgoCD ApplicationSet deploys anihpj to both clusters. Git drives configuration. Networking: Route53 latency-based routing → nearest cluster. Health checks auto-failover. Observability: Prometheus per cluster + Thanos for global query. Grafana with cluster dropdown variable. DR: RDS read replica in DR region. Active-passive: EKS primary, GKE standby. Failover: Route53 detects EKS unhealthy → routes to GKE. Platform: Backstage shows services across both clusters transparently.

Explanation

Complete multi-cloud architecture. CNPA values: unified control plane, GitOps for consistency, cloud-agnostic tooling (ArgoCD, Crossplane, Prometheus). The platform abstracts cloud differences — developers deploy to "production," platform routes to the right cloud.

Chapter 21: Crossplane — Kubernetes-Native Infrastructure Management

Crossplane turns Kubernetes into a universal control plane for infrastructure. Instead of Terraform scripts, you define cloud resources as Kubernetes YAML — and manage them with kubectl, GitOps, and all your existing K8s tooling.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~1.5 hours ✈️ Crossplane 🎯 Domain 4: 12%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Crossplane architecture: XRDs, Compositions, Managed Resources
  • ✅ Crossplane vs Terraform — when to use each
  • ✅ Building a self-service Platform API for anihpj with Crossplane

21.1 What is Crossplane? — The Cloud Control Plane

Crossplane extends Kubernetes with Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) that represent cloud resources. You define your own platform APIs (e.g., "PostgreSQL database") and Crossplane provisions the actual cloud resources (RDS, Cloud SQL, etc.) behind the scenes.

Crossplane — Developer Request → Cloud Resource
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                      │
  │  ① Developer: "I need a PostgreSQL database"                         │
  │     kubectl apply -f my-database.yaml                                │
  │     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐              │
  │     │ apiVersion: platform.anihpj.io/v1alpha1          │              │
  │     │ kind: PostgreSQL                                 │              │
  │     │ spec: { size: small, version: "14" }            │              │
  │     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘              │
  │                             │                                        │
  │                             ▼                                        │
  │  ② Crossplane XRD + Composition (Platform-defined template)          │
  │     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐              │
  │     │ Composition maps PostgreSQL →                   │              │
  │     │   • AWS RDS Instance (db.t3.small)              │              │
  │     │   • Security Group (allow 5432)                 │              │
  │     │   • K8s Secret (connection string)              │              │
  │     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘              │
  │                             │                                        │
  │                             ▼                                        │
  │  ③ Cloud resources provisioned automatically                         │
  │     ✅ RDS instance created + Security Group + K8s Secret injected    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

21.2 Crossplane vs Terraform — When to Use Which

DimensionTerraformCrossplane
ApproachDeclarative HCL, state fileK8s-native, continuous reconciliation
Control LoopPlan → Apply (discrete)Continuous (K8s reconciliation loop)
Self-ServiceLimited (via Terraform Cloud)Built-in (kubectl, GitOps, Backstage)
Drift DetectionTerraform plan (on demand)Continuous (every reconciler loop)
Best ForInitial provisioning, Day 0Ongoing management, Day 1+, self-service
ComplementTerraform provisions the K8s clusterCrossplane manages everything inside + cloud resources

21.3 Building a Platform API with Crossplane for anihpj

1
Install Crossplane

helm install crossplane crossplane-stable/crossplane -n crossplane-system

2
Install AWS Provider

Apply Provider + ProviderConfig with cloud credentials

3
Define XRD

Create CompositeResourceDefinition for "Database" type

4
Define Composition

Map "Database" → RDS Instance + SecurityGroup + K8s Secret

5
Developer Self-Service

kubectl apply -f my-db.yaml → Crossplane provisions everything!

📝 Crossplane Composition YAML

Database Composition for anihpj
apiVersion: apiextensions.crossplane.io/v1
kind: Composition
metadata: { name: postgresql.anihpj.io }
spec:
  compositeTypeRef:
    apiVersion: platform.anihpj.io/v1alpha1
    kind: XPostgreSQL
  resources:
    - name: rds-instance
      base:
        apiVersion: rds.aws.upbound.io/v1beta1
        kind: Instance
        spec:
          forProvider:
            instanceClass: db.t3.small
            engine: postgres
            engineVersion: "14"
            region: us-east-1
    - name: connection-secret
      base:
        apiVersion: kubernetes.crossplane.io/v1alpha1
        kind: Object
        spec:
          forProvider:
            manifest:
              apiVersion: v1
              kind: Secret
              metadata: { namespace: anihpj-prod }
              data:
                endpoint: "rds-instance.endpoint"

✅ Chapter 21 Summary — Crossplane — K8s-Native Infrastructure

You've mastered Crossplane, the Kubernetes-native infrastructure management tool. Unlike Terraform (which runs outside K8s in CI/CD), Crossplane runs inside your cluster and uses CRDs to represent cloud resources. Key concepts: XRD (Composite Resource Definition — your custom API), Composition (the blueprint that maps your API to cloud resources), Managed Resources (the actual cloud resources Crossplane creates). For the anihpj platform, a developer creates an XPostgreSQL YAML, Crossplane provisions an RDS instance + Kubernetes Secret — no Terraform knowledge needed. This is the essence of Domain 4: self-service infrastructure APIs.

✈️ Key Takeaway 1

Crossplane = K8s-native IaC. Terraform = external IaC. Crossplane runs reconciliation loops inside K8s, uses CRDs, and fits GitOps natively.

✈️ Key Takeaway 2

XRD = define your API (e.g., XPostgreSQL). Composition = define how to provision it. Managed Resource = the actual cloud resource created.

✈️ Key Takeaway 3

Crossplane enables true developer self-service: dev writes YAML, platform defines what that YAML provisions. No tickets, no wait time, no infra expertise needed.

📝 Chapter 21 — CNPA Practice Questions (Crossplane — K8s-Native Infrastructure)

Q1
What is Crossplane and how is it fundamentally different from Terraform?
Show Answer
Answer

Crossplane is a Kubernetes-native infrastructure-as-code tool that runs INSIDE a K8s cluster using CRDs and reconciliation loops. Key differences from Terraform: (1) Crossplane runs inside K8s continuously reconciling; Terraform runs externally as a CLI during CI/CD. (2) Crossplane uses K8s CRDs; Terraform uses HCL. (3) Crossplane fits natively into GitOps (ArgoCD/Flux); Terraform needs Terraform Cloud/Atlantis. (4) Crossplane allows developer self-service via kubectl; Terraform workflow is external. Both manage cloud resources, but Crossplane is "K8s-native" while Terraform is "cloud-agnostic external."

Explanation

CNPA Domain 4: "What runs inside K8s for infrastructure?" → Crossplane. Key differentiator: reconciliation loop runs continuously, not just at plan/apply time. Crossplane = K8s watches the cloud; Terraform = CI/CD pushes to the cloud.

Q2
What are XRD, Composition, and Managed Resource? How do they work together?
Show Answer
Answer

Three-layer architecture: XRD (Composite Resource Definition): Defines YOUR custom API — what developers see. e.g., XPostgreSQL with field storageGB: 100. Composition: The blueprint that maps your XRD to actual cloud resources. "When someone creates an XPostgreSQL, provision: RDS Instance + SecurityGroup + SubnetGroup + K8s Secret." Managed Resource: The actual cloud resource Crossplane creates and manages (e.g., an RDS instance in AWS). Flow: Dev creates Claim → XRD validates → Composition selects blueprint → Managed Resources are provisioned → K8s Secret with connection details.

Explanation

CNPA MUST know: XRD = custom API, Composition = blueprint, Managed Resource = actual cloud resource. This is the essence of platform engineering: platform team defines XRD+Composition once, developers create Claims forever.

Q3
What is a reconciliation loop? How does Crossplane use it?
Show Answer
Answer

Reconciliation loop: Observe (check desired state in CRD vs actual state in cloud) → Diff (calculate what needs to change) → Act (call cloud API to converge) → Repeat (continuously). Crossplane controllers run this loop forever. If someone manually changes an RDS instance in AWS console, Crossplane detects the drift and re-converges it back to the desired state defined in the CR. This is the Kubernetes control loop pattern applied to cloud infrastructure. Terraform only reconciles when you run terraform apply.

Explanation

CNPA: "What pattern does Crossplane use?" → Reconciliation loop (Observe→Diff→Act). This is why Crossplane is "self-healing" — it continuously fixes drift. Terraform detects drift on plan but only fixes on apply.

Q4
How does Crossplane enable developer self-service for the anihpj platform?
Show Answer
Answer

Platform team creates XRD (e.g., XPostgreSQL) and Composition (maps to RDS). Developer writes: apiVersion: platform.anihpj.io/v1alpha1; kind: XPostgreSQL; spec: { storageGB: 100, engineVersion: "14" }. Runs kubectl apply -f my-db.yaml. Crossplane provisions: RDS instance, security group, subnet group, K8s Secret (anihpj-db-creds). Developer's app references the Secret. Zero cloud knowledge needed. No ticket to platform team. No Terraform. No AWS console. This is the platform promise: "developers consume, platform provides."

Explanation

Self-service is Domain 4's core. CNPA: "How does Crossplane enable self-service?" → Platform defines API (XRD+Composition), devs consume via kubectl. The platform abstracts cloud complexity behind a K8s-native interface.

Q5
What is a ProviderConfig? How does Crossplane authenticate to cloud providers?
Show Answer
Answer

ProviderConfig contains cloud credentials and configuration. For AWS: references a K8s Secret containing aws_access_key_id and aws_secret_access_key (or IRSA — IAM Roles for ServiceAccounts). Specifies: region, IAM role ARN. For GCP: references Secret with GCP service account key. For Azure: Secret with azure.json (client ID, client secret, subscription ID). Multiple ProviderConfigs = multi-cloud from one Crossplane. Best practice: use Workload Identity (GCP), IRSA (AWS), or AAD Pod Identity (Azure) instead of static credentials.

Explanation

CNPA: "How does Crossplane connect to clouds?" → ProviderConfig + K8s Secret with credentials. IRSA/Workload Identity recommended over static keys. One Crossplane instance can manage AWS, GCP, and Azure simultaneously via separate ProviderConfigs.

Q6
How does Crossplane integrate with ArgoCD/Flux for GitOps?
Show Answer
Answer

Crossplane resources are K8s CRDs → they work natively with GitOps: (1) Store XRD definitions, Compositions, Claims, and ProviderConfigs in Git. (2) ArgoCD/Flux watches the Git repo. (3) When a new XPostgreSQL claim is committed, ArgoCD syncs it to the cluster. (4) Crossplane detects the new claim and provisions the RDS instance. (5) The resulting K8s Secret is auto-committed back? No — Secrets stay in-cluster; connection details are read by apps. This is "GitOps for infrastructure" — the entire cloud footprint is defined in Git and reconciled by Crossplane. No separate Terraform pipeline needed.

Explanation

CNPA: "How does Crossplane fit GitOps?" → CRDs are K8s resources → GitOps tools sync them natively. This is the advantage over Terraform: no external state file, no separate pipeline. Everything is K8s-native, Git-driven.

Q7
What is a Composite Resource Claim (XRC) and how does it differ from XRD?
Show Answer
Answer

XRD (Composite Resource Definition): Defines the schema — the "class." Platform team creates this once. XRC (Composite Resource Claim): An instance created by a developer — the "object." Think: XRD = class definition, XRC = instance. XRC is namespace-scoped, XRD is cluster-scoped. When a dev runs kubectl apply -f my-db.yaml with kind XPostgreSQL, they create an XRC. Crossplane creates the corresponding Composite Resource (XR, cluster-scoped) behind the scenes. The XR manages the actual Managed Resources.

Explanation

CNPA: "XRC vs XRD?" → XRD = schema, XRC = instance. Namespace-scoped claim vs cluster-scoped definition. Decouples developer's namespace from cluster-wide infrastructure management.

Q8
What is Upbound and how does it relate to Crossplane?
Show Answer
Answer

Upbound is the company behind Crossplane. Upbound offers: (1) Upbound Console: UI for managing Crossplane resources across clusters. (2) Upbound Registry: Marketplace for pre-built XRD+Composition packages. (3) Upbound Cloud: Managed control planes (hosted Crossplane). (4) Official Providers: AWS, GCP, Azure providers maintained by Upbound (upbound.io/provider-aws). Crossplane = open-source CNCF project. Upbound = commercial offerings built on Crossplane. Similar to: Kubernetes (CNCF) vs GKE/EKS/AKS (managed).

Explanation

CNPA: "What is Upbound?" → Company behind Crossplane, offers managed control planes and pre-built providers. Crossplane is the open-source CNCF project. Upbound providers are the standard way to manage cloud resources.

Q9
How does Crossplane handle drift detection and self-healing?
Show Answer
Answer

Crossplane's reconciliation loop continuously compares desired state (CRD) with actual state (cloud API). If someone manually changes an RDS instance (e.g., changes instance class in AWS console), Crossplane detects: "CRD says db.t3.small, AWS says db.t3.large → drift!" Crossplane automatically reverts the change back to the desired state. This is self-healing. With Terraform, you'd need to run terraform plan to detect drift and terraform apply to fix it. Crossplane's continuous reconciliation means drift is fixed automatically within the resync interval (default 1 minute).

Explanation

Drift detection is a key Crossplane advantage. CNPA: "How does Crossplane handle manual cloud changes?" → Continuous reconciliation detects drift and self-heals. Terraform only detects drift on plan; Crossplane detects and fixes continuously.

Q10
Design anihpj's platform API with Crossplane: what XRDs, Compositions, and self-service workflow would you create?
Show Answer
Answer

XRDs: XPostgreSQL (database), XRedis (cache), XS3Bucket (object storage), XKafka (messaging). Compositions: Each XRD has a Composition that maps to the best cloud service for that environment (AWS RDS, GCP Cloud SQL, Azure DB). Developer self-service: Dev creates: kind: XPostgreSQL; spec: { storageGB: 50, version: "15", environment: "staging" } → Crossplane provisions PostgreSQL + SecurityGroup + monitoring dashboards + K8s Secret. Platform policy: Compositions enforce: encryption at rest (mandatory), backup retention (30 days min), instance sizing limits, region constraints (GDPR data residency). GitOps: All platform APIs in Git → ArgoCD syncs → Crossplane reconciles. Result: developers get cloud resources in 60 seconds without opening a ticket.

Explanation

This is the CNPA vision of platform engineering. Platform defines composable, policy-enforced APIs via Crossplane. Developers consume them via kubectl. Cloud complexity hidden. Governance built-in. Fully GitOps-native.

🎯 EXAM HOTSPOT — Crossplane & Platform APIs (Domain 4, 12%)

Key CNPA facts: (1) Reconciliation loop: Observe → Diff → Act → Repeat — Crossplane's controllers continuously reconcile desired state (CRD) with actual state (cloud). (2) XRD vs Composition vs Managed Resource: XRD = your custom API (what devs see), Composition = blueprint (how to provision), Managed Resource = actual cloud resource. (3) Crossplane vs Terraform: Crossplane runs INSIDE K8s (CRDs, GitOps-native). Terraform runs OUTSIDE K8s (HCL, CI/CD). (4) ProviderConfig: Connects Crossplane to a cloud account (AWS IAM, GCP SA, Azure SP). (5) Self-service pattern: Developer creates claim → Crossplane provisions → connection Secret auto-created → app uses Secret.

Chapter 22: Hybrid and Edge Platform Engineering

Not everything runs in a public cloud. This chapter covers hybrid cloud patterns, GitOps for edge computing, Cluster API for declarative cluster management, and platform federation — managing many clusters as one.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~1 hour 🌐 Hybrid 🎯 Domain 4: 12%

22.1 Hybrid Cloud Patterns

Hybrid cloud combines on-premises infrastructure with public cloud — driven by data sovereignty, latency requirements, existing data center investments, or burst-to-cloud capacity needs.

Hybrid Platform Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              🏗️ UNIFIED PLATFORM CONTROL PLANE (Cloud-Hosted)        │
  │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐               │
  │  │ Git Repos│ │Backstage │ │  ArgoCD  │ │ Grafana  │               │
  │  └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘               │
  └────────┬──────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
           │                              │
           ▼                              ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────┐
  │  🏢 ON-PREM DC   │        │  ☁️ AWS CLOUD     │
  │  ┌────────────┐  │        │  ┌────────────┐  │
  │  │ K8s Cluster│  │  VPN/  │  │ EKS Cluster│  │
  │  │ (Bare Metal)│◀─┼─DC─────┼─▶│ (us-east-1)│  │
  │  │            │  │        │  │            │  │

  │  └────────────┘  │        │  └────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────┘        └──────────────────┘

22.2 GitOps for Edge Computing

Edge computing presents unique challenges: intermittent connectivity, resource constraints, and massive scale (hundreds or thousands of locations). GitOps is the ideal management pattern for edge because each cluster reconciles independently from Git — no constant connection to a central control plane needed.

Edge GitOps — Central Git → 1000 Edge Clusters

  │          │                 │                 │                      │
  │          ▼                 ▼                 ▼                      │

  │   │ ┌─────────┐ │  │ ┌─────────┐ │  │ ┌─────────┐ │                │

22.3 Cluster API — Declarative Cluster Lifecycle Management

Cluster API (CAPI) manages the lifecycle of Kubernetes clusters — using Kubernetes itself. Think of it as "Deployments for clusters": define a desired cluster spec, and CAPI creates, scales, upgrades, and deletes clusters across any infrastructure provider.

📝 Chapter 22 — CNPA Practice Questions (Hybrid & Edge Platform Engineering)

Q1
What is Hybrid Platform Engineering? Why is K8s ideal for hybrid deployments?
Show Answer
Answer

Hybrid platform engineering combines on-premises, edge, and public cloud infrastructure into a unified platform. K8s is ideal because: (1) Consistent API — same kubectl commands work everywhere. (2) Portable workloads — container images run the same on-prem, cloud, edge. (3) GitOps — ArgoCD/Flux deploy identically to any cluster. (4) Service mesh — Istio abstracts cross-cluster networking. (5) Managed control planes + self-managed workers — hybrid architectures possible. Key challenge: latency, bandwidth, network partitions between sites.

Explanation

CNPA Domain 5: "Why K8s for hybrid?" → consistent API + portable containers + GitOps. The platform abstracts location so apps don't care where they run. Hybrid = on-prem + cloud. Multi-cloud = multiple public clouds.

Q2
What is Edge Computing and why is K3s the preferred edge K8s distribution?
Show Answer
Answer

Edge computing runs workloads close to data sources (IoT devices, retail stores, factories) to minimize latency. K3s is ideal for edge because: (1) Small footprint: ~50MB binary vs ~500MB for full K8s. (2) Lightweight: Uses SQLite (not etcd) for storage. (3) Single binary: Server + agent in one binary. (4) ARM64 support: Runs on Raspberry Pi, ARM edge devices. (5) Auto-deploying manifests: Drops manifests in /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/. (6) Helm controller built-in. Ideal for: oil rigs, retail stores, autonomous vehicles, 5G cell towers. NOT ideal for: large datacenter clusters.

Explanation

CNPA: "K8s for edge?" → K3s (Rancher/SUSE). Lightweight, single binary, SQLite, ARM support. Edge needs: low resource usage, offline resilience, GitOps-based deployment (Flux preferred for edge).

Q3
What is Cluster API (CAPI)? How does it enable hybrid cluster lifecycle management?
Show Answer
Answer

Cluster API (CAPI) brings K8s-style declarative APIs to cluster lifecycle management. Instead of running eksctl create cluster or gcloud container clusters create, you define a Cluster YAML and apply it. Workflow: Define Cluster + Infrastructure objects → CAPI controller provisions VMs, installs K8s, joins nodes → Cluster is ready. Infrastructure Providers: AWS (CAPA), GCP (CAPG), Azure (CAPZ), vSphere (CAPV), OpenStack (CAPO). Bootstrap Providers: Kubeadm (CABPK). Control Plane Providers: KubeadmControlPlane (KCP), or managed (EKS, AKS, GKE). CAPI + ArgoCD = GitOps for entire clusters.

Explanation

CNPA: "Declarative cluster lifecycle?" → Cluster API. Key: clusters become K8s resources managed by GitOps. CAPI provisions clusters on-prem AND cloud using different infrastructure providers but the same API.

Q4
Why is GitOps ideal for edge and hybrid? Compare ArgoCD vs Flux for edge.
Show Answer
Answer

GitOps is ideal for edge/hybrid because: (1) Declarative desired state in Git — single source of truth. (2) Pull-based reconciliation works even with intermittent connectivity. (3) Self-healing — if drift occurs, agent reverts to Git state. (4) All changes audited via Git history. Flux for edge: Lighter weight, no UI, uses SOPS for secrets, smaller footprint. Better for resource-constrained edge. ArgoCD: Feature-rich UI, multi-cluster management, ApplicationSets. Better for centralized multi-cluster management. Both support pull-based reconciliation — the agent polls Git, not Git pushing to agents. Important for edge behind NAT/firewalls.

Explanation

CNPA: "GitOps for edge?" → Flux (lightweight, pull-based). Edge challenges: intermittent connectivity, limited resources, NAT. GitOps agents pull from Git → works behind firewalls, survives network outages.

Q5
What is Platform Federation? How do you manage 100 clusters as one platform?
Show Answer
Answer

Platform Federation treats multiple clusters as a single logical platform. Strategies: (1) ArgoCD Multi-Cluster: One ArgoCD control plane deploys Applications to many clusters. ApplicationSets template deployments across clusters. (2) Crossplane: Infrastructure federation — one Crossplane manages cloud resources across accounts/regions. (3) Service Mesh Federation: Istio multicluster connects services across clusters (same mesh, different clusters). (4) Karmada/KubeFed: Multi-cluster workload distribution. (5) Unified Observability: Thanos/Cortex for multi-cluster metrics, centralized Loki for logs. Key: consistent policies, consistent security, consistent developer experience across ALL clusters.

Explanation

CNPA: "Manage many clusters as one?" → Federation via ArgoCD (apps), Crossplane (infra), Istio (networking). Goal: developer doesn't know or care which cluster their app runs on. The platform federates transparently.

Q6
What is KubeFed and how does it differ from Karmada for multi-cluster?
Show Answer
Answer

KubeFed (Kubernetes Federation v2): Original multi-cluster project. Propagates K8s resources across clusters using FederatedDeployment, FederatedService, etc. Template + Placement + Override pattern. Status: deprecated/less active. Karmada: CNCF sandbox project, more modern approach. Key features: (1) Multi-cluster scheduling with policies (spread, aggregate, static weight). (2) Resource propagation across clusters. (3) Override policies for per-cluster customization. (4) Better cluster failure handling. Karmada is the spiritual successor to KubeFed. CNPA prefers Karmada for modern multi-cluster architectures.

Explanation

CNPA: "Multi-cluster workload distribution?" → Karmada (preferred) or KubeFed (legacy). These go beyond ArgoCD multi-cluster: they SCHEDULE workloads across clusters based on policies (resource availability, latency, region).

Q7
What is the Hub-Spoke architecture for multi-cluster management?
Show Answer
Answer

Hub-Spoke: Hub cluster: Runs management tools (ArgoCD, Crossplane, Thanos, centralized logging). Developer interacts with hub only. Spoke clusters: Run actual workloads. Each spoke is an independent K8s cluster (could be on-prem, cloud, edge). Hub deploys to spokes via ArgoCD multi-cluster. Spokes report metrics to hub (Thanos receive). Spokes report logs to hub (Loki). Benefits: (1) Single pane of glass for all clusters. (2) Spoke clusters can be isolated (air-gapped, different networks). (3) Hub failure doesn't affect spoke workloads. (4) Each spoke can be different K8s flavor (EKS, GKE, K3s).

Explanation

CNPA: "Architecture for managing many clusters?" → Hub-Spoke. Hub = management. Spokes = workloads. Hub deploys to spokes, spokes report back. Critical: spoke workloads keep running even if hub is down. GitOps enables this pattern naturally.

Q8
What are the challenges of edge K8s and how do you solve them?
Show Answer
Answer

Edge K8s challenges: (1) Limited resources: Solution → K3s (small binary) or MicroK8s. (2) Intermittent connectivity: Solution → local container registry mirror, GitOps pull model, local storage. (3) No on-site expertise: Solution → zero-touch provisioning, automated recovery, remote management via hub. (4) Security: Solution → hardware root of trust, signed images, locked-down OS (Flatcar, Bottlerocket). (5) Updates: Solution → over-the-air (OTA) updates, dual-partition A/B updates (like Android). (6) Monitoring: Solution → push metrics to hub when connectivity allows, buffer locally. (7) Heterogeneity: ARM64 vs AMD64, GPU vs no GPU. Solution → multi-arch images.

Explanation

Edge is CNPA Domain 5. Key challenges: resources, connectivity, management, security. K3s + GitOps (Flux) + local registry = standard edge stack. Think: "What if the cluster runs on an oil rig with satellite internet?"

Q9
How does Flux handle edge deployments with image automation?
Show Answer
Answer

Flux image automation at edge: (1) Flux ImageRepository: watches container registry for new image tags matching a pattern (e.g., semver: 1.x). (2) Flux ImagePolicy: selects the latest image matching policy (e.g., semver range, filter). (3) Flux ImageUpdateAutomation: automatically updates Git repo with new image tag when detected. This creates a Git commit → Flux reconciles → edge clusters pull new image. For edge: (a) Registry mirror caches images locally on edge LAN. (b) Flux can deploy even when hub Git is unreachable (last known state). (c) Commit back to Git provides audit trail. (d) SOPS decrypts secrets locally at edge.

Explanation

CNPA: "Image automation for edge?" → Flux ImageRepository + ImagePolicy + ImageUpdateAutomation. Auto-update Git on new image → edge eventually reconciles. Edge registry mirror caches images. Works even with intermittent connectivity.

Q10
Design anihpj's hybrid-edge platform architecture: HQ cluster + 50 retail store edge clusters.
Show Answer
Answer

HQ Hub (GKE Autopilot): ArgoCD (manifests for all clusters), Crossplane (cloud infra for HQ), Thanos (metrics from all edges), Loki (logs from all edges), Grafana (unified dashboards), Kyverno (policies replicated to all edges). Edge (50 K3s clusters): Each store: 3 Raspberry Pi nodes running K3s + Flux (pull from HQ Git), local registry mirror, Point-of-Sale app, inventory DB, local Prometheus + Grafana Agent (push to HQ). GitOps: HQ Git repo → per-store folder with Kustomize overlays for store-specific config. Flux at each store pulls and reconciles. Resilience: Store apps run locally even if HQ connectivity lost. Buffer metrics/logs locally, push when reconnected. Updates: Flux image automation detects new POS app image → updates Git → edge Flux reconciles → rolling update. Security: Signed images, Kyverno policies enforced locally, mTLS for store-to-HQ comms.

Explanation

Complete hybrid-edge architecture. Hub = centralized management. Edge = autonomous operation. GitOps connects them. Critical: edge functions WITHOUT hub. This is the CNPA vision for Domain 5: hybrid and edge platforms.

🔴 Part 8: Service Mesh & API Gateways Chapters 23-24

Chapter 23: Service Mesh Concepts and Architecture

A service mesh is an infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication. It moves reliability, security, and observability from application code into the platform — giving you mTLS, retries, circuit breaking, and traffic splitting without developers writing a single line of code.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2 hours 🕸️ Service Mesh 🎯 Domain 4: 12%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What a service mesh is and why platforms need one
  • ✅ Istio (Envoy-based) vs Linkerd (Rust micro-proxy) — when to use each
  • ✅ Traffic management: canary, A/B testing, circuit breaking, retries, timeouts, fault injection
  • ✅ Zero-code observability with service mesh

23.1 What is a Service Mesh and Why Do Platforms Need One?

A service mesh is an infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication. It consists of a data plane (sidecar proxies next to each pod) and a control plane (manages configuration and policy). The key insight: reliability moves from app code → platform layer.

Service Mesh — Before & After
  ❌ WITHOUT SERVICE MESH:
  ┌─────────┐    direct HTTP     ┌─────────┐
  │ Service A│──────────────────▶│ Service B│
  │ (anihpj)│    no encryption   │ (auth)   │
  └─────────┘                    └─────────┘
  • No mTLS between services • Retries in app code • No circuit breaking

  ✅ WITH SERVICE MESH (Istio/Linkerd):
  ┌─────────┐      mTLS        ┌─────────┐
  │ anihpj  │                  │  auth   │
  │ ┌─────┐ │  ┌──────────┐   │ ┌─────┐ │
  │ │ app │─┼─▶│ sidecar  │───┼▶│ app │ │
  │ └─────┘ │  │ (Envoy/  │   │ └─────┘ │
  └─────────┘  │ linkerd) │   └─────────┘
               └────┬─────┘
                    │
               ┌────┴────┐
               │ Control │  ← Policy, mTLS certs, telemetry config
               │ Plane   │
               └─────────┘
  ✅ Auto mTLS ✅ Built-in retries/circuit breaking ✅ Traffic splitting

23.2 Istio — The Most Popular Service Mesh

Istio uses Envoy as its sidecar proxy and Istiod as its control plane. Key CRDs: VirtualService (routing rules), DestinationRule (load balancing, connection pools, mTLS), PeerAuthentication (enforce mTLS STRICT or PERMISSIVE).

Istio Architecture — Control Plane + Data Plane
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                        ☸️ KUBERNETES CLUSTER                         │
  │                                                                      │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  🧠 ISTIOD (Control Plane)                                     │   │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐                    │   │
  │  │  │ Pilot    │  │ Citadel  │  │ Galley   │                    │   │
  │  │  │(routing) │  │(certs)   │  │(config)  │                    │   │
  │  │  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘                    │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                             │ xDS API (dynamic config)               │
  │                             ▼                                        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  🚀 DATA PLANE (Envoy Sidecars)                               │   │
  │  │                                                               │   │
  │  │  ┌─────────┐  mTLS + metrics  ┌─────────┐                    │   │
  │  │  │ anihpj  │                  │  auth   │                    │   │
  │  │  │ ┌─────┐ │  ┌──────────┐   │ ┌─────┐ │                    │   │
  │  │  │ │ app │─┼─▶│  Envoy   │───┼▶│ app │ │                    │   │
  │  │  │ └─────┘ │  │ (sidecar)│   │ └─────┘ │                    │   │
  │  │  └─────────┘  └────┬─────┘   └─────────┘                    │   │
  │  │                    │  Traces → Jaeger                         │   │
  │  │                    │  Metrics → Prometheus                    │   │
  │  │                    │  Logs → stdout (collected by Fluentd)    │   │
  │  └────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                       │                                              │
  │  ┌────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  🌐 INGRESS GATEWAY (Istio Gateway)                            │   │
  │  │  External traffic → Gateway → VirtualService → anihpj         │   │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Istio VirtualService — Canary: 90% v1, 10% v2
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata: { name: anihpj }
spec:
  hosts: [anihpj]
  http:
    - route:
        - destination:
            host: anihpj
            subset: v1
          weight: 90     # 90% traffic to v1
        - destination:
            host: anihpj
            subset: v2
          weight: 10     # 10% traffic to v2 (canary)

23.3 Linkerd — The Lightweight Alternative

Linkerd is written in Rust, uses a micro-proxy (~10MB memory per pod, vs Envoy's ~50MB+), and is dramatically simpler than Istio (fewer CRDs, easier to operate).

DimensionIstioLinkerd
ProxyEnvoy (C++)linkerd-proxy (Rust)
Memory/Pod~50-100MB~10MB
CRDs50+~5
Traffic Splitting✅ VirtualService✅ SMI TrafficSplit
mTLS✅ Per-mesh or per-service✅ Automatic, always-on
Best ForLarge orgs, complex routingSimplicity-first, low resource

23.4 Traffic Management with Service Mesh

a) Canary Deployments

Route a percentage of traffic to new version, monitor, gradually increase. Istio VirtualService weight field controls the split. Start 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% based on metrics.

b) A/B Testing (Header-Based Routing)

Route users to different versions based on HTTP headers. Example: match: headers: { user-agent: { regex: ".*Mobile.*" } } → send mobile users to v2.

c) Circuit Breaking

Stop sending requests to a failing service. Istio DestinationRule sets connectionPool and outlierDetection (eject failing pods for 30s after 5 consecutive 5xx errors).

d) Retries

Automatically retry failed requests. VirtualService retries: { attempts: 3, perTryTimeout: 2s }. The mesh retries — not your application code.

e) Timeouts

Prevent waiting forever. VirtualService timeout: 5s — if the backend doesn't respond in 5 seconds, the mesh returns a 504.

f) Fault Injection

Test resilience by deliberately injecting failures. VirtualService fault: { delay: { percentage: 10, fixedDelay: 5s } } — 10% of requests get 5s delay. Test your circuit breakers!

💡 Platform Engineer's Insight

All six traffic management patterns are configured via YAML — no application code changes. This is the power of a service mesh: the platform team defines reliability patterns, and every service inherits them automatically.

23.5 Observability with Service Mesh

The mesh provides zero-code observability. Since every request flows through the sidecar proxy, you get metrics, traces, and service graphs without instrumenting your application.

ToolWhat It ProvidesIntegration
KialiService graph visualization — see all services and their traffic flowIstio-native
JaegerDistributed tracing — follow requests across servicesBuilt into Istio
GrafanaPre-built Istio dashboards (traffic, latency, errors)Via Prometheus
PrometheusRequest count, latency (P50/P95/P99), error rate — auto-collectedIstio metrics endpoint

✅ Chapter 23 Summary — Service Mesh Deep Dive

You've mastered the service mesh — the infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication without application code changes. You compared Istio (feature-rich, Envoy-based) to Linkerd (lightweight, Rust-based) to Cilium (eBPF-based, no sidecars), and learned the six traffic management patterns every platform engineer should know: canary deployments, A/B testing, circuit breaking, retries, timeouts, and fault injection. The key insight: a service mesh moves reliability logic from application code to platform infrastructure — developers get it for free, and platform engineers control it centrally.

🕸️ Key Takeaway 1

Service mesh = east-west traffic (service-to-service). API Gateway = north-south traffic (external → cluster). Together they cover all traffic.

🕸️ Key Takeaway 2

Sidecar (Istio/Linkerd) vs sidecarless (Cilium/eBPF). Sidecars add latency but are proven. eBPF is newer, faster, but less mature.

🕸️ Key Takeaway 3

Six patterns: canary, A/B, circuit break, retry, timeout, fault injection — ALL configured via YAML, zero code changes. Platform team defines, dev team inherits.

📝 Chapter 23 — CNPA Practice Questions (Service Mesh Deep Dive)

Q1
What is a Service Mesh? How does it differ from an API Gateway?
Show Answer
Answer

A service mesh is an infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service (east-west) communication transparently. It adds mTLS, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, and observability without application code changes. API Gateway handles north-south traffic (external clients → cluster) and adds API management features: rate limiting, authentication, request transformation, developer portal. Together: API Gateway at the edge, service mesh inside the cluster. For anihpj: Kong/Ambassador handles external API traffic, Istio/Linkerd handles internal microservice communication.

Explanation

CNPA Domain 4: "Service mesh vs API Gateway?" → Mesh = east-west (service-to-service), Gateway = north-south (external-to-cluster). They complement each other. Know the direction of traffic for each.

Q2
What is the Sidecar Pattern? What are the tradeoffs vs Sidecarless (eBPF)?
Show Answer
Answer

Sidecar (Istio/Linkerd): A proxy container injected into each pod alongside the app container. Handles all network traffic. Pros: battle-tested, isolated proxy crash doesn't kill app, per-pod fine-grained policies. Cons: doubles pod count, adds latency (~1-5ms per hop), higher memory usage (~50-100MB per sidecar). Sidecarless (Cilium/eBPF): eBPF programs run in kernel, no separate container. Pros: no sidecar overhead, lower latency, less memory. Cons: newer technology, requires kernel 5.10+, harder to debug. CNPA expects understanding of both approaches.

Explanation

CNPA: "Sidecar vs sidecarless?" → Sidecar = separate proxy container (Istio/Linkerd). Sidecarless = kernel-level eBPF (Cilium). Sidecar = more mature, more overhead. eBPF = newer, faster, less overhead. The trend is toward sidecarless.

Q3
What is mTLS and why does a service mesh provide it automatically?
Show Answer
Answer

mTLS (mutual TLS) encrypts traffic AND authenticates both sides. In a service mesh: every sidecar proxy gets an identity certificate (SPIFFE format: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/anihpj-sa). Istiod distributes certs. Sidecars automatically establish mTLS for all pod-to-pod traffic. No application code changes needed. Benefits: (1) Encryption everywhere — all traffic encrypted in transit. (2) Authentication — both sides verified cryptographically. (3) Authorization — policies based on identity, not IP. (4) Zero-trust networking — no trust based on network location. Key: the platform provides this; developers don't implement TLS in their apps.

Explanation

CNPA: "What provides automatic encryption between services?" → mTLS via service mesh. Istio/Linkerd auto-issue certs, auto-rotate, auto-encrypt. This is the "zero-trust" networking model for microservices. No application-level TLS needed.

Q4
What is Circuit Breaking? How do you configure it in Istio?
Show Answer
Answer

Circuit breaking stops sending requests to a failing service to prevent cascading failures (similar to an electrical circuit breaker). In Istio, configured via DestinationRule: trafficPolicy: connectionPool: { tcp: { maxConnections: 100 }, http: { http1MaxPendingRequests: 50 } }; outlierDetection: { consecutive5xxErrors: 5, interval: 30s, baseEjectionTime: 30s, maxEjectionPercent: 50 }. This means: after 5 consecutive 5xx errors, eject the pod for 30 seconds. Max 50% of pods ejected at once. The failing service gets time to recover while requests are routed to healthy pods.

Explanation

Circuit breaking prevents cascading failures. CNPA: "What prevents cascading failures?" → Circuit breaking (DestinationRule). Key params: consecutive5xxErrors, baseEjectionTime, maxEjectionPercent. Without it, one failing service can take down the entire system.

Q5
What is a Canary Deployment? How does Istio VirtualService implement traffic splitting?
Show Answer
Answer

Canary deployment routes a small percentage of traffic to a new version, monitors it, then gradually increases. Istio VirtualService: http: - route: - destination: { host: anihpj, subset: v1, weight: 90 }; - destination: { host: anihpj, subset: v2, weight: 10 }. This sends 90% to v1, 10% to v2 (the canary). Monitor: error rate, P99 latency, CPU. If canary is healthy → increase to 25% → 50% → 100%. If canary shows errors → rollback (set v2 weight to 0). This is more sophisticated than K8s rolling update because: (1) you control traffic %, not pod count %. (2) You can monitor and decide. (3) Rollback is instant (just change weight).

Explanation

Canary = gradual traffic shift based on metrics. CNPA: "How to do canary deployment?" → Istio VirtualService weight field. Key: you shift TRAFFIC, not pods. K8s rolling update shifts pods; Istio canary shifts traffic. Much safer.

Q6
Compare Istio, Linkerd, and Cilium for service mesh. When would you choose each?
Show Answer
Answer

Istio: Most feature-rich, Envoy-based sidecar. Best for: large enterprises needing full feature set (mTLS, traffic management, authorization, telemetry, multi-cluster). Cons: complex, high resource usage. Linkerd: Rust-based sidecar, simpler deployment, lower resource. Best for: teams wanting "just works" service mesh with minimal complexity. Cons: fewer features than Istio. Cilium: eBPF-based, NO sidecars. Best for: performance-sensitive workloads, large clusters, teams wanting kernel-native networking. Cons: newer, requires kernel 5.10+, eBPF debugging complexity. Decision: Istio for features, Linkerd for simplicity, Cilium for performance.

Explanation

CNPA: "Which service mesh for...?" → Istio (features), Linkerd (simplicity), Cilium (performance, eBPF). All provide: mTLS, traffic management, observability. Choose based on: complexity tolerance, performance requirements, platform maturity.

Q7
What is Fault Injection and how does it improve platform resilience?
Show Answer
Answer

Fault injection deliberately introduces failures to test system resilience. Istio VirtualService: fault: { delay: { percentage: { value: 10 }, fixedDelay: 5s } }; { abort: { percentage: { value: 5 }, httpStatus: 500 }}. This injects: 10% of requests get 5s delay, 5% get HTTP 500. Purpose: (1) Test that circuit breakers work. (2) Test that retries work. (3) Test that timeouts work. (4) Test that fallback mechanisms work. (5) Chaos engineering — break things on purpose in staging to verify resilience. Key: NEVER in production (use chaos mesh for controlled chaos). Staging-only fault injection to validate resilience before production incidents.

Explanation

CNPA: "How to test resilience?" → Fault injection (delay + abort). Inject failures in staging to verify circuit breakers, retries, timeouts all work. "Chaos engineering" light. Don't use in production — use dedicated chaos tools there.

Q8
What are Retries and Timeouts? Why define them in the mesh, not the app?
Show Answer
Answer

Retries: Automatically re-attempt failed requests. Istio: retries: { attempts: 3, perTryTimeout: 2s, retryOn: "5xx,connect-failure" }. Mesh retries up to 3 times, each attempt max 2s. Timeouts: Maximum time to wait for response. Istio: timeout: 5s. If backend doesn't respond in 5s, mesh returns 504. Why in mesh not app: (1) Consistent across all services. (2) No language-specific implementation. (3) Platform controls reliability policies centrally. (4) Can adjust without redeploying apps. (5) Works for services written in any language. The mesh handles transient failures so your app code stays simple.

Explanation

Reliability in the mesh, not the app. CNPA: "Why retry in mesh?" → language-agnostic, centrally managed, no app changes. Key values: attempts + perTryTimeout + retryOn. Without retries: transient network glitch = user sees error.

Q9
What is A/B Testing? How does header-based routing work in Istio?
Show Answer
Answer

A/B testing routes users to different versions based on request characteristics (not random %). Istio VirtualService: match: - headers: { end-user: { exact: "test-user" } }; route: - destination: { host: anihpj, subset: v2 }. Traffic from "test-user" goes to v2, everyone else to v1. Use cases: (1) Internal teams test v2 with header x-canary: true. (2) Route mobile users to one version, desktop to another. (3) Beta program: users with group: beta get new features. (4) Geographic routing: EU users → EU cluster. Unlike canary (random %), A/B is deterministic based on request attributes. Often used together: canary for gradual rollout, A/B for targeted testing.

Explanation

CNPA: "A/B testing vs canary?" → A/B = header-based routing (deterministic), canary = weighted routing (random %). Both configured via VirtualService. A/B is great for: beta programs, mobile vs desktop, geographic routing.

Q10
Design the complete service mesh strategy for anihpj: which mesh, traffic patterns, observability.
Show Answer
Answer

Mesh: Istio (full-featured, enterprise-ready). Alternative: Cilium if performance-critical. Security: mTLS everywhere (STRICT mode), all pod-to-pod encrypted. AuthorizationPolicy: deny by default, allow by named service accounts. Traffic: Canary for production releases (10%→50%→100%), circuit breaking (5 consecutive 5xx → 30s ejection), retries (3 attempts, 2s timeout each), timeouts (5s default API timeout), fault injection (staging only). Observability: Kiali (service graph, traffic visualization), Jaeger (distributed tracing — trace requests across services), Prometheus + Grafana (RED metrics: Rate, Errors, Duration per service). Multi-cluster: Istio multicluster for HQ+edge deployment. anihpj-specific: jobpost service (P1) → canary + circuit breaking. User service → mTLS + retries. All services → RED dashboards in Grafana. Platform team defines all mesh config; services inherit automatically.

Explanation

Complete mesh architecture. CNPA: mesh = security (mTLS) + reliability (circuit, retry, timeout) + observability (Kiali, Jaeger, Prometheus). Platform defines once, all services inherit. This is the promise of a service mesh.

🎯 EXAM HOTSPOT — Service Mesh (Domain 4, 12%)

The CNPA exam tests service mesh fundamentals: (1) North-South vs East-West: Ingress/API Gateway = north-south (external → cluster). Service Mesh = east-west (service-to-service). (2) Data Plane vs Control Plane: Data plane = sidecar proxies (Envoy/Linkerd-proxy) handling actual traffic. Control plane = management layer (Istiod/Linkerd control plane) distributing config. (3) Sidecar vs Sidecarless: Istio/Linkerd use sidecars (one proxy per pod). Cilium uses eBPF (kernel-level, no sidecars). Sidecarless = lower latency, lower resource usage. (4) mTLS: Automatic mutual TLS between all services — encrypts ALL pod-to-pod traffic without application changes. (5) Six traffic patterns every platform engineer should configure centrally: canary, A/B, circuit breaking, retries, timeouts, fault injection.

24.2 Popular API Gateways for Kubernetes

a) Kong

Open-source, Lua-based, massive plugin ecosystem (200+). Runs on Kubernetes with Kong Ingress Controller. Best for: enterprises needing auth, rate limiting, transformations, and API analytics in one platform.

b) Ambassador (Emissary)

Kubernetes-native, Envoy-based, CRD configuration. Mappings define routes. Best for: K8s-native teams who want API gateway as K8s YAML.

c) Gloo Edge (Solo.io)

Envoy-based with powerful request/response transformation. Supports function-level routing (Lambda, Cloud Functions). Best for: hybrid/multi-cloud with serverless integration.

d) APISIX (Apache)

High-performance (NGINX-based), rich plugin system, dynamic configuration via etcd. Best for: performance-critical API gateways handling millions of requests.

e) Traefik

Built-in Let's Encrypt, auto-discovery of K8s services, simple configuration. Best for: simplicity-first, automatic HTTPS, small-to-medium deployments.

As a platform engineer, you provide the API management infrastructure so service teams can publish, secure, and monitor their APIs consistently.

🎯 CNPA Exam Tip

Know the difference: Ingress = basic L7 routing (host/path → Service), API Gateway = full API management (auth, rate limiting, developer portal), Service Mesh = east-west service-to-service (mTLS, retries, circuit breaking). They complement each other — a mature platform uses all three.

📝 Rate Limiting for anihpj API (Kong Example)

Kong Ingress + Rate Limiting Plugin
apiVersion: configuration.konghq.com/v1
kind: KongPlugin
metadata:
  name: rate-limit-anihpj
plugin: rate-limiting
config:
  minute: 100        # 100 requests per minute per consumer
  policy: local
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  annotations:
    konghq.com/plugins: rate-limit-anihpj
spec:
  rules:
    - host: api.anihpj.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /jobs
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: anihpj
                port: { number: 8000 }

📝 Chapter 24 — CNPA Practice Questions (API Gateways & Ingress Controllers)

Q1
What is an API Gateway? How does it differ from a basic Ingress Controller?
Show Answer
Answer

An API Gateway manages north-south traffic (external→cluster) with full API management features. Ingress Controller: Basic L7 routing (host/path → service). NGINX Ingress, Traefik. API Gateway: Everything Ingress does PLUS: authentication (API keys, JWT, OAuth2), rate limiting, request/response transformation, API versioning, developer portal, analytics, monetization. Examples: Kong, Ambassador, Gloo, APISIX. For anihpj: Ingress routes api.anihpj.io to the anihpj service. API Gateway adds: rate limiting (100 req/min per API key), JWT validation, API documentation portal for partners.

Explanation

CNPA Domain 4: "Ingress vs API Gateway?" → Ingress = basic routing. API Gateway = routing + auth + rate limiting + API lifecycle management. API Gateway is a SUPERSET of Ingress functionality with API management features.

Q2
What are the 5 stages of the API lifecycle for platform teams?
Show Answer
Answer

API lifecycle for platform teams: (1) Design: Define API contract using OpenAPI/Swagger spec. Store in Git. Lint and validate in CI. (2) Publish: Deploy API to gateway, expose in developer portal (Backstage). Developers discover and subscribe. (3) Secure: Apply authentication (API keys, OAuth2, JWT), rate limiting, IP allowlists. Gateway enforces; services don't implement auth. (4) Monitor: Track RED metrics (Rate, Errors, Duration) per API. Set alerts for anomalies. Dashboard per API consumer. (5) Deprecate: Announce sunset with Sunset HTTP header, 6-month migration window, versioned APIs (/v1/, /v2/). Platform provides infrastructure at every stage.

Explanation

CNPA: "What are the API lifecycle stages?" → Design → Publish → Secure → Monitor → Deprecate. Platform provides tools at each stage. The API Gateway is the central enforcement point for stages 2, 3, and 4.

Q3
What is Kong? Compare Kong, Ambassador, and Gloo for API Gateway.
Show Answer
Answer

Kong: Most popular open-source API Gateway. Built on NGINX/OpenResty. Plugin-based architecture: 200+ plugins for auth, rate limiting, logging, transformation. Declarative config via CRDs (Kong Ingress Controller) or DB mode. Ambassador: Built on Envoy Proxy. K8s-native, CRD-based configuration. Good for: Emissary-Ingress users, teams wanting Envoy-based gateway. Gloo: Solo.io product. Envoy-based, advanced features: GraphQL support, API transformation, WASM plugins. More enterprise-focused. Comparison: Kong = most plugins, largest community. Ambassador = simple, K8s-native. Gloo = most features (but more complex). All three handle: auth, rate limiting, routing, transformation, observability.

Explanation

CNPA: "Which API Gateway?" → Kong (most plugins, largest community), Ambassador (K8s-native, Envoy), Gloo (advanced, enterprise). All are K8s-native API Gateways that go beyond basic Ingress. Know at least one for the exam.

Q4
What is Rate Limiting? How does an API Gateway implement it?
Show Answer
Answer

Rate limiting restricts how many requests a client can make in a time window. Purpose: (1) Protect backend services from overload. (2) Enforce fair usage (especially for free tier APIs). (3) Prevent abuse/DDoS. (4) Monetization (different rate limits for different tiers). Kong plugin: rate-limiting: config: { minute: 100, hour: 1000, policy: local }. Algorithms: token bucket, sliding window, fixed window. Platform pattern: Gateway enforces rate limits; backend services don't need rate-limiting code. Client gets 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After header. Rate limit by: IP, API key, consumer, endpoint. Redis backend for distributed rate limiting across gateway replicas.

Explanation

CNPA: "How to protect backends from overload?" → Rate limiting via API Gateway. Key: gateway enforces, services stay simple. Distributed rate limiting uses Redis. 429 + Retry-After header. Platform concern, not application concern.

Q5
What is an OpenAPI Specification? How does it enable the API-first approach?
Show Answer
Answer

OpenAPI (formerly Swagger) is a machine-readable API specification format (YAML/JSON). Defines: endpoints, parameters, request/response schemas, authentication methods. API-first approach: (1) Write OpenAPI spec FIRST (before code). (2) Generate interactive docs (Swagger UI). (3) Generate client SDKs (openapi-generator). (4) Generate server stubs. (5) Validate requests/responses against spec. (6) Use spec to configure API Gateway routing + validation. For anihpj: anihpj-api.yaml defines all endpoints, stored in Git. Kong reads spec to auto-configure routes + validation. CI pipeline: lint spec → validate backwards compatibility (no breaking changes) → deploy → update developer portal.

Explanation

CNPA: "What is OpenAPI?" → Machine-readable API definition. Enables: docs generation, SDK generation, validation, gateway configuration. API-first = spec before code. Platform uses spec to auto-configure gateway routes + validation.

Q6
How does an API Gateway handle Authentication (API Key, JWT, OAuth2)?
Show Answer
Answer

Gateway authenticates before traffic reaches backend: (1) API Key: Simple. Client includes X-API-Key: abc123. Gateway validates against key store. Good for: machine-to-machine, internal APIs. (2) JWT: Client includes Authorization: Bearer <jwt>. Gateway validates: signature (using JWKS), expiry, issuer, audience. No database lookup needed. Good for: user-facing APIs, microservices. (3) OAuth2: Full authorization flow. Gateway acts as Resource Server — validates access tokens against Authorization Server. Good for: third-party integrations. Kong plugin: jwt: { claims_to_verify: [exp, iss] }. Key: Backend services never see auth logic — they receive verified user context in headers (e.g., X-User-ID).

Explanation

CNPA: "Gateway authentication methods?" → API Key, JWT, OAuth2. Gateway validates at the edge; backend trusts headers. This is the platform pattern: auth is a platform concern, services get clean user context. No auth code in applications.

Q7
What is a Developer Portal? How does Backstage serve as one?
Show Answer
Answer

A Developer Portal is the self-service hub where developers discover, learn about, and subscribe to APIs. Backstage (Spotify/CNCF): Extensible developer portal. Shows: (1) All available APIs with OpenAPI docs. (2) API ownership (which team). (3) API status (health, uptime). (4) API subscription (request API key). (5) Rate limits and usage. (6) SDK downloads. For anihpj: Backstage portal at dev.anihpj.io. Teams publish APIs; other teams discover and consume. No more "who owns the user API? what's the endpoint? how do I get an API key?" — everything is in the portal. Key: self-service API discovery reduces platform team support burden.

Explanation

CNPA: "Developer portal?" → Backstage (CNCF). Central hub for API discovery, docs, subscription. Platform builds the portal; teams publish APIs. Self-service discovery = fewer "how do I use X?" tickets for platform team.

Q8
What is Ingress NGINX vs Gateway API? Why is Gateway API the future?
Show Answer
Answer

Ingress (networking.k8s.io/v1): Basic L7 routing. One resource type. Simple host/path→service mapping. Limitations: single controller, limited features, annotation spaghetti. Gateway API (gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1): Next-gen K8s networking. Multiple resources: GatewayClass (which controller), Gateway (listener config), HTTPRoute (routing rules), ReferenceGrant (cross-namespace). Benefits: (1) Role-based — infra team manages Gateway, dev team manages HTTPRoute. (2) Expressive — header-based routing, traffic splitting, mirroring. (3) Portable — same API across different implementations (Istio, NGINX, Envoy). (4) Multi-tenancy — different teams manage their routes independently. Gateway API is the future; Ingress is the legacy.

Explanation

CNPA: "Ingress vs Gateway API?" → Gateway API = more expressive, role-based, portable. Know the resources: GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute. Gateway API separates concerns: platform manages Gateway, developers manage HTTPRoutes.

Q9
What is Request/Response Transformation in an API Gateway?
Show Answer
Answer

API Gateways can modify requests and responses on the fly without changing backend code: (1) Request transformation: Add/remove headers, rewrite paths (e.g., /api/v2/users → /users), add query parameters, validate request body against schema. (2) Response transformation: Remove sensitive headers (e.g., Server, X-Powered-By), add CORS headers, transform XML→JSON, aggregate multiple backend responses into one. Kong: request-transformer and response-transformer plugins. Benefits: (1) Backend services stay simple. (2) Transformations applied consistently. (3) Can modernize legacy APIs without changing legacy code. (4) Add security headers (HSTS, CSP) centrally.

Explanation

Gateway as a transformation layer. CNPA: "Modify requests without app changes?" → Request/Response transformation plugins. Platform handles: header management, path rewriting, security headers, CORS. Services focus on business logic.

Q10
Design anihpj's API management strategy: gateway, auth, portal, lifecycle, and observability.
Show Answer
Answer

Gateway: Kong (200+ plugins, large community) or Ambassador (Envoy-native). Deployed via Helm, configured via CRDs. Routing: Gateway API with HTTPRoute. api.anihpj.io → Kong Gateway → anihpj services. Auth: JWT for user APIs (OIDC from Keycloak/Auth0). API keys for partner integrations. OAuth2 for third-party apps. Rate Limiting: 100 req/min free tier, 1000 req/min paid tier. Per consumer. Redis backend for distributed counting. Portal: Backstage at dev.anihpj.io. All APIs documented with OpenAPI specs. Self-service subscription. Lifecycle: OpenAPI spec in Git → CI validates → Kong auto-configures → Deploy → Monitor in Grafana → SunSet header for deprecation. Observability: Prometheus metrics from Kong plugin (rate, errors, latency per API per consumer). Grafana dashboards. Alerts on: 429 spike, 5xx increase, high latency.

Explanation

Complete API management strategy. CNPA: API Gateway = the unified enforcement point for routing, auth, rate limiting, transformation, and observability. Platform manages the gateway; teams manage their API definitions.

📋 Part 8 Summary — Service Mesh & API Gateways

🕸️
Service Mesh

Infrastructure layer for service-to-service comms. Data plane (sidecar proxy) + control plane. Istio (Envoy, feature-rich) vs Linkerd (Rust, lightweight).

🚦
Traffic Management

Canary, A/B testing, circuit breaking, retries, timeouts, fault injection — all via YAML. Zero code changes. Platform defines; services inherit.

🌐
API Gateways

Kong, Ambassador, Gloo, APISIX, Traefik. North-south traffic + API management. Complement service mesh (east-west) and ingress (basic routing).

FinOps (Financial Operations) is the cloud financial management discipline that brings together Engineering, Finance, and Product teams to make data-driven spending decisions. It's not about cutting costs — it's about maximizing business value per cloud dollar spent.

25.2 Kubernetes Cost Management

Kubernetes resource requests and limits are the primary cost drivers. Over-provisioned pods waste 30-50% of cloud spend at scale.

Optimization LeverTypical SavingsDifficulty
Right-sizing requests/limits30-50%🟡 Medium
Spot/Preemptible nodes60-80%🟢 Easy
Reserved/Savings Plans30-50%🟢 Easy
Schedule dev shutdown (nights/weekends)50-65%🟢 Easy
Delete unused resources (volumes, IPs, LBs)10-20%🟢 Easy
ARM/Graviton migration20-40%🔴 Hard
Autoscaling (HPA + Karpenter)25-40%🟡 Medium

25.3 Cost-Aware Platform Design

Build cost controls into the platform so teams don't have to think about them. Resource Quotas and Limit Ranges prevent cost runaway; spot instances reduce spend on fault-tolerant workloads.

ResourceQuota + LimitRange for anihpj
# Limit total resources per namespace (cost guardrail)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata: { name: anihpj-quota, namespace: anihpj-dev }
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "20"
    requests.memory: 40Gi
    limits.cpu: "40"
    limits.memory: 80Gi
    persistentvolumeclaims: "10"
---
# Set default requests/limits for all pods
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata: { name: anihpj-limits, namespace: anihpj-dev }
spec:
  limits:
    - default: { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }
      defaultRequest: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
      type: Container

  │  ┌──────┴──────┐                                                     │
  │  │ YES         │ NO                                                  │
  │  ▼             ▼                                                     │
  │  Can handle    Steady-state workload?                                │

  │  │YES  │NO     ▼             ▼                                       │

  │        and │         │                                                │
  │                                                                      │

25.4 Chargeback and Showback Models

Showback

Show teams their costs without billing them. Increases awareness. "Your team spent $3,200 this month on compute." No payment required. Start here.
